plan.chapter_thesis: Metasurface holographic displays have transitioned from static wavefront engineering to dynamic system prototypes, yet their commercial readiness remains constrained by the uncoupled optimization of inverse design algorithms, fabrication scalability, and active modulation integration.
plan.reader_takeaway: While inverse design and hybrid architectures enable complex holographic functionalities, the field's primary bottleneck is no longer single-component performance but the system-level integration required to achieve real-time refresh rates, full-color gamuts, and wide eye-boxes simultaneously.

argument_sequence.purpose: Establish the foundational role of computational inverse design in overcoming high-dimensional design spaces for holographic wavefronts.
Detail advanced algorithmic frameworks (hybrid, adjoint, generative) that address non-uniqueness and efficiency in metasurface synthesis.
Define the core display architectures (transmissive/reflective) and the shift toward hybrid meta-refractive systems for compactness.
Demonstrate specific functional capabilities enabled by inverse design, such as multi-channel multiplexing and polarization control.
Address critical barriers: design complexity crosstalk, non-uniqueness in manufacturing, and the ill-posed nature of the inverse problem.
Explore dynamic modulation mechanisms beyond static designs, including microfluidics and symmetry-breaking approaches.
Evaluate application readiness, specifically highlighting AR waveguides and identifying gaps in full-system metrics like refresh rate and eye-box.

terminology_rows.note: Computational approach mapping desired optical responses to structural parameters using optimization or ML.
Integration of governing physical equations into neural network loss functions to ensure physical realizability.
System combining metasurfaces for aberration correction with refractive elements for optical power.
Resonant states with theoretically infinite quality factors used for dynamic modulation via symmetry breaking.

explanation_block_rows.title: The Computational Imperative: Inverse Design Foundations
explanation_block_rows.goal: Introduce the necessity of inverse design methods for navigating the high-dimensional parameter space of holographic metasurfaces, contrasting them with traditional analytical approaches.

explanation_block_rows.title: Algorithmic Evolution: From Adjoint Methods to Generative Models
explanation_block_rows.goal: Explain how hybrid algorithms, adjoint optimization, and generative models overcome the limitations of local minima and non-uniqueness in design.

explanation_block_rows.title: System Architectures: Transmissive, Reflective, and Hybrid Integrations
explanation_block_rows.goal: Categorize current display implementations and highlight the emergence of hybrid meta-refractive lenses as a solution for compact, high-quality imaging.

explanation_block_rows.title: Functional Multiplexing: Polarization, Wavelength, and Channel Control
explanation_block_rows.goal: Demonstrate specific capabilities achieved through inverse design, such as quad-channel outputs and polarization conversion, which are critical for full-color displays.

explanation_block_rows.title: Design Bottlenecks: Non-Uniqueness, Crosstalk, and Manufacturability
explanation_block_rows.goal: Analyze the fundamental trade-offs where increased design complexity leads to channel crosstalk and manufacturing ambiguity due to one-to-many mappings.

explanation_block_rows.title: Dynamic Frontiers: Microfluidics and Symmetry-Breaking Modulation
explanation_block_rows.goal: Shift focus from static to dynamic systems, evaluating mechanisms like microfluidics and BIC symmetry breaking for real-time adaptability.

explanation_block_rows.title: Application Readiness: AR Waveguides and Remaining System Gaps
explanation_block_rows.goal: Assess the proximity to commercial deployment, citing AR waveguide successes while identifying unresolved gaps in refresh rates and eye-box uniformity.
